segments.text: Chapter 4 — Callie: Fifteen Days to Meridian
They should have been on the causeway by ten in the morning.

Callie had been building toward that for four days, and she had said it out loud to all of them twice, and everybody had agreed, and it had been, up until about half past eight, an extremely good plan.
At half past eight her mother
could not be woken up.
It lasted a little under two minutes, and for most of it Callie was not in her own body at all.

Her mother lay on the wagon boards with her eyes half open and did not answer to her name, and her right hand went on doing a small plucking motion at the blanket, over and over, the same motion, as if she were picking at a thread that was not there.
Then she stopped.
Then she took a long breath and looked up at all four of them standing over her and said, in a perfectly ordinary voice, "What."
Nobody said anything.
"What," her mother said again, and then, with the first edge of something under it, "Callie, what."
"You went off for a minute."
"I did not."
"You did."
Her mother looked at the sky for a while.
"Well," she said.
That's new."
They lost the morning to it.

They lost it because she was sick after, and then sick again, and then could not keep water down, and Pell would not put the wagon on a road with her like that and Katori would not overrule him, and Callie — who wanted more than anything in the world to be moving — found that she agreed with both of them and hated it.
By the time her mother could sit up and hold a cup it was two in the afternoon.

By the time they came up out of the scrub onto the reservoir road it was past five, and the light was going long and gold and sideways, and the Fenner flats opened out in front of them, two miles of cracked grey pan with the causeway running dead straight across the middle of it like a seam.
Callie went out to the head of it alone and read the ground, and came back, and by then she already knew what she was going to have to say.
"It's crossing," she said.
Katori put the brake on.
"Where."
"Everywhere.
That's the problem."
Callie crouched and drew it in the dust with the end of the hook, because she needed her hands doing something.
"The whole flat drains north-east.
Everything that comes across this country comes across that, and it walks the low pan until it hits the embankment, and the embankment's the only grade in eleven miles.
So it goes up.
It always goes up.
This isn't a line crossing the road, it's — the road is where the line ends up."
"How fresh."
"There's sign at the head that's from this morning and there's sign a hundred paces on that's from about an hour ago."
"And the far side?"
"Two miles.
I can't see the far side.
Nobody can see the far side from here, that's the whole thing about it."
Katori stood on the board with her hands on the rail and looked north along the causeway for a long time.
"All right," she said.
"Which is worse."
"What?"
"You heard me.
I'm not asking you what's dangerous, I know what's dangerous.
I'm asking you which of the two things we can actually do is worse.
On the causeway at dusk, or camped on this pan, beside a line, in the dark, until morning."
Callie's mouth was very dry.
She did the arithmetic.
She made herself do all of it, the way her grandfather had made her do it in ditches, out loud where somebody could catch her getting it wrong.
Camped on the pan meant no fire and no walls and a hundred directions and eleven hours.
The causeway meant one direction, one wide, twenty feet of broken rock on both sides that nothing could come up fast
, and two miles, which with a wagon was about fifty minutes.
It also meant no turning.
That was the whole cost and she made herself say it.
"The causeway," she said.
"There's no turning on it.
If it's bad in the middle we go forward or we go nowhere, and I want that said before anybody agrees with me."
"Said," Katori agreed.
"Pell."
Pell already had the pencil out.
He wrote for a moment, and then turned the book around so Callie could see it, and there in the small neat hand at the bottom of the day's page was: Causeway at dusk.
C.'s call.
Concur — K., P.
"That's not to blame you with," Pell said.
"That's so that in a year when somebody says it was a fool's decision I can show them the three of us made it together and what we knew when we made it."
He put the pencil behind his ear.
"Get up on the wagon and don't walk the first half mile.
I want you fresh at the far end, not the near one."
They were eleven hundred paces on when the first one came up the rock.

Callie had spent the whole of that eleven hundred paces up on the crate stack with her legs hanging and her eyes going left and right down the riprap, and she saw it while it was still four rocks below the shoulder — a grey-brown shape hauling itself up the broken stone on all four points, going straight up the slope because a husk has no idea that a slope has an easy way and a hard way.
"East side," she said.
"One.
Coming up."
Ines was on the bed before the sentence finished.
"Sixty," she said.
"Fifty-five."
"Let it come up," said Katori, from the front.
"Don't spend an arrow on one."
And that was
the last decision anybody got to make with time to spare in it.
Because the first one was not one.

The first one was the first, which is a completely different thing, and by the time it got its hands over the shoulder of the embankment there were four more below it on the east rock and six on the west and a long smear of movement out on the pan that Callie could not count and did not try to.
"Mass on the west," she said.
Her voice came out much steadier than she was.
"West is the mass.
East is three, four — east is small."
"Heard," said Katori.
"Otto, west.
Pell, hold their heads, don't you dare let them run.
Ines, the bed.
Callie — "
"Back."
"Back."
Here is what the causeway gave them, and it was more than they had any right to.
It was one wagon wide.

The husks could not spread and they could not surround, because there was nowhere to be except in front or behind, and the wagon itself sat across the middle of it like a plug in a pipe with about two feet of gap at each wheel.

And on both sides the embankment fell away twenty feet in loose broken rock at an angle no husk could climb without putting all four points down and committing every bit of its weight into the going-up.
A husk on that rock could not brace.
It had nothing to brace with and no sense to want to.
Callie learned that in the first fifteen seconds and it reorganized everything she thought she knew.
The first one at her end came over the shoulder on the east side with its long arms out and its head down, and she did not swing at it.
She put the hook over the top of its shoulder from the outside, set her back foot on the road, and leaned, and the whole weight of it went back the way it had come.
It did not fall so much as unhappen.

It went down the riprap on its back with its arms still reaching, and it hit the second one coming up four rocks below, and took it, and the pair of them went down together in a long grinding slide to the pan.
Neither of them came apart.
Neither of them died.
They got up down there, both of them, and started up again.
It did not matter.
It had cost her one second and a pull, and it had cost them ninety feet of climbing, and while they were climbing they were not on her road.
"Don't kill them," she shouted forward.
"Tip them — don't kill them —"
Nobody heard her.
There was too much noise by then.
At the front, Katori was killing them.
Callie saw it in pieces, over her shoulder, between pulls.

Katori had put herself eight paces ahead of the team with the road all to herself, and the grey blade was in her hand, and she was working with her elbow in and her feet barely moving, one short stroke per husk, under the arm and out.
The bodies came apart almost before they finished arriving.
She did not step back once.
She was magnificent and she was
making it worse with every single one, and Callie understood that a full four seconds before she understood why, in the way you sometimes solve a thing with your stomach before your head catches up.
The ash.

It came apart into that fine drifting grey that does not blow away, and it came down on the deck, and the deck had a camber on it, and the ash went where water would have gone — sideways, to the low edge, running down the crown of the road in long pale tongues and pooling against the rail stubs and the wheel ruts and gathering there, silver and shining and going nowhere.
Ash brings more.
Everybody said so.
Everybody said it the same flat way people say things they have watched happen.

And on the other side of the same coin there was a lit woman standing in the middle of an empty grey pan at dusk doing the single brightest thing anybody in eleven miles could do, and Callie had been told what that meant too, by a man at Gaunt's Reach who had been the kind of man who would have been there.
Two things in the world bring them.
Both of them were ours.
Both of them were
the exact thing keeping everybody alive for the next thirty seconds.
That was the trap and there was no way out through the front of it.
"Katori!"
she screamed.
"Stop putting it down!"
"Nine," said Ines.
She was up on the crate stack with her feet planted apart and she loosed and it went into a husk coming over the west shoulder and the thing sat down, and the next one climbed over it.
"Six."
"Where's four and five?"
Otto bellowed.
"Gone.
West rock, I'm not going down there."
She loosed.
"Four."

Otto had the wagon pole, which was eight feet of seasoned hickory with an iron collar on the end, and he was not fighting with it so much as sweeping the west shoulder — short flat strokes at the height of a knee, catching them as they came over the lip, and every one he caught went back down the rock and took time with it.
He had it exactly right and Callie had not told him a word of it.
He had watched her do it for two minutes and copied it.
"Two."
"Make them count," said Katori.
"I've been making them count for eleven years."
"None," said Ines, eight seconds later, and put the bow down on the crates with a care that under any other circumstances would have been funny, and picked up the skillet.
The mule went over at about the four-minute mark.
Callie did not see how.

She heard Pell shouting — a high, cracked, appalling sound out of a man who had not raised his voice once in nine days — and she turned in time to watch the whole wagon lurch a foot and a half sideways as the traces went slack on one side, and then the mule was simply not there, and there was a noise from down on the rock that she put away somewhere and did not take out again for a long time.
The wagon slewed.
The off rear wheel came up onto a rail stub at the edge and hung.
And the two feet of gap at the wheel
became four.

And on the near side of the pole, still harnessed, still buckled into a trace that now ran twenty feet down a slope of broken rock to a weight that was not going to move again, the horse went out of her mind.
Pell had her head.

He had both hands in the cheekpieces and his boots planted and he was talking to her the entire time in a low, level, unbroken voice that never once went up at the end, and he was not going to be able to hold her, and everybody on that road knew it including Pell.
She got her hook into one in the gap and pulled it down and put her boot on its neck, and that was the first one she actually killed, and the ash of it went out across the deck and joined the rest.
The second one in the gap she caught badly.

It came up the east rock faster than it should have, low, on three points, and she swung the hook down into the seam of its shoulder at full reach and full commitment, and the steel went in, and the husk went sideways off the rock all at once, and the hook went with it.
She had four feet of conduit in her hands and a wing nut.

Callie stood on the shoulder of the causeway and looked down twenty feet of broken rock at her grandfather's hook, wedged between two slabs with a dead grey shape coming apart around it, and there was
no part of the decision in her at all.
She went down after it.
It took eleven seconds and it was the stupidest thing she had ever done.

She went down on three points the way they did, and got her boot wedged, and got it back, and reached the hook and hauled it out of the slabs with both hands and a noise she did not hear herself make.
She was starting back up when her mother said her name.
Not screamed it.
Said it.

The wagon bed was above and behind her, up past the lip of the embankment, out of her sight entirely, and across all of that noise, in a voice that had no strength left in it to be loud with, her mother said, "Callie," in the tone of somebody who has just seen the shape of the next four seconds and is
letting go of them.
Callie came up over the lip of the causeway on her hands and knees.
Two of them were over the tailgate.

They had come up the rear of the embankment while the whole world was looking at the gap, and they were on the bed, in among the crates, three feet from where her mother lay with her back against the boards.
Twenty-two feet of wagon between them.
Callie ran.

She went up the near side, past the wheel, past the crates, past Ines coming the other way with a skillet in both hands, and she did not look at the horse because the horse was not the thing that was killing her mother, and that was the entire mistake and it was a completely reasonable one.
Duchess came around on the pole.
There was no warning in it.

That was the thing Callie could never make anybody understand afterward — that a horse does not tell you, that the ears and the eye and all the rest of it are for other horses and not for you, and that four hundred kilos of terrified animal tied by the neck to a dead weight hanging off a cliff does not decide anything at all.
It was not aimed at her.
It was simply the direction that was available.
She saw the near hind come up off the deck at the height of her chest.
And Callie did the oldest thing there is.
She did not duck and she did not step and she did not do one single one of the things eleven years of her grandfather's teaching had put into her body.
She threw her arms up in front of her face, the way a child does, the way anybody does, and she shut her eyes.
Something closed over her.
It went down.
That was the part she could never say.
It did not go up and it did not go out and it did not come from anywhere in the direction she had thrown her arms.
It went down, underneath her, deeper than a girl goes — and it had been there the whole time.
It was not warm and it was not light and it was not kind.

It was enormous and it was patient and it had been lying under her all her life the way bedrock lies under a field, and she had walked around on top of it for thirteen years and never once put her hand through.
Four hundred miles she had pulled a barrow with two lengths of cargo strapping crossed over her ribs.
She had never in all that time considered that the weight might be the small part.
Something took the other side of the yoke and pulled with her.
The hoof hit.
It hit a hand's breadth off her forearm, and it stopped.
Not slowed.
Not turned.

There was a sound like a maul coming down on a green stump, one flat enormous note with nothing after it, and the whole of that kick went into something a finger's width off Callie's skin and went absolutely nowhere, and nothing came through it.
Not the force.
Not the shock of it.
Her arms did not move.
Her boots did not slide on the deck.
Duchess did.
The horse came off it.
Four hundred kilos of animal at the end of a full kick rebounded off a thirteen-year-old girl standing in a road, and staggered sideways into the pole with her hindquarters, and screamed.
Callie stood with her arms still up over her face and her eyes still shut.
It was on her.
That was the only word she had and it was not the right one.

It was closed over her from her boots to the crown of her head, a skin's thickness off her everywhere at once, and she could feel it the way you feel a coat — not as a thing out in front of her, but as a thing she was wearing — and she understood, with a clarity that had no explanation anywhere behind it, that she could not get it off.
And in her right hand the hook went cold.
Cold the way the inside of a well is cold.
She opened her eyes and looked at it, and it was not four feet of conduit and a foot of forged curve any more.
The curve kept going.

It came out past where the steel stopped, grey and flat and the colour of nothing at all, following the line her grandfather's hook had been making for sixty years and then simply going on with it — three feet of it, four, hanging out over the deck, a long ugly wrong-shaped sweep of edge coming off a farm tool that had no business doing anything whatsoever.
It was not a sword.
Callie had seen a sword twice in her life and it was not one.
She had not chosen a single thing about it.
She turned and went down the length of the wagon with both of them.
The first husk at the tailgate she took off the boards with a pull, and it came apart in the air.

The second one she caught under the arm at a reach she had never had in her life, from further away than her arms went, and it stopped being a shape all at once and from everywhere, the way a knot comes out when you pull the right end.
Her mother lay against the crates with her hand up in front of her face, staring at her daughter, and said nothing at all.
The rest of it took about four minutes and Callie was not really present for any of them.
She knew afterward that Katori had got the mass turned at the front.
That Otto had held the west shoulder one-handed with a crate lid and his forearm open from elbow to wrist.
That Ines had put three husks off the bed with a cast-iron skillet and been extremely calm about it.

That Pell had stood at the head of one ruined horse for eleven minutes with a dead trace hanging off the other side of her and had not let go, and had not stopped talking, and had never once let his voice go up at the end.
She knew she had killed nine of them at the tailgate, because she had counted, because she always counted.

She also knew that three of them had come straight into her, hard, in the middle of all that — one of them at a flat run off the top of a crate — and that she had not so much as rocked back on her heels, and that they had come off her the way water comes off a stone.
Then it stopped.
It stopped the way it always stops, which is not with any kind of signal.

There was nothing coming up the rock, and then there went on being nothing coming up the rock, and the noise went out of the world piece by piece until all that was left was one horse breathing very fast and Otto being sick over the west rail and the long dry hiss of ash running down the camber of the road.
The last of the light was off the pan.
The causeway ran north into blue dark in front of them and south into blue dark behind them, and there was ash lying silver in every seam of it for forty paces in both directions.
Callie stood in the middle of it.
The hook was still wrong.
She had been holding it for four minutes and it had not stopped.

When she turned her wrist the long grey sweep of it turned too, and went through the air without any weight in it at all, and she could feel that it was hers the way she could feel her own tongue in her own mouth.
And the other thing was still shut over her.
She could see perfectly well through it.
She had walked eleven paces in it and it had come with her, every step, the way a coat comes with you.
The ash running down the camber of the road reached her boots and did not touch them.
It parted, and went around her, and closed up again on the downhill side, and left her standing in a clean dry shape of road exactly the size of a girl.
She was holding both of them.
At the same time.
She could feel the weight of each one separately, and she knew — without one single person ever having told her anything about any of it — that she was not supposed to be able to.
"Katori," she said.
Katori had come up the length of the wagon and stopped about six feet away.
Her Ember was still out.

There was grey ash all the way up both her arms and across her face, and she had not put her blade away, and she was not looking at the ash and she was not looking at the horse and she was not looking at Otto's arm.
She was looking at the thing closed over Callie.
And then at the hook.
And then back at the thing closed over Callie.
"Katori."
Callie's voice came apart on her.
"I can't put it down.
Either of them.
I can't — "
She stopped, because she did not know how the sentence ended.
"Which one is it?"
she said.
Katori did not answer her.

She did not answer her for a long time, and the not-answering went on and on, out there in the dark in the middle of two miles of road with nowhere at either end of it to turn around — while the ash came down the camber and parted around a girl's boots and closed up behind them, and the hook her grandfather had used to swing grain sacks went on being four feet longer than it had ever been in its life.
